raw_text:
Atrial fibrillation (AF) is a major cause of ischaemic stroke, and most thrombi in non-valvular AF arise from the left atrial appendage (LAA) [1], [2]. The LAA is anatomically variable, trabeculated and contractile; stasis, endothelial dysfunction and hypercoagulability make it a rational mechanical target, particularly when thrombus has been excluded by transoesophageal echocardiography or cardiac computed tomography [3]. Stroke and bleeding risk estimation with CHA2DS2-VASc and HAS-BLED remains central to decision-making [4], [5]. Although direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) are first-line therapy for most eligible patients and have improved the therapeutic ratio compared with warfarin [6], [7], [8], percutaneous LAA closure has emerged for patients with high thromboembolic risk in whom long-term anticoagulation is undesirable, unsafe or unacceptable.

The evidence base began with the WATCHMAN randomized programme. In PROTECT AF, LAA closure was non-inferior to warfarin for a composite of stroke, systemic embolism and cardiovascular death, but early procedural complications—particularly pericardial effusion—were important [9]. Subsequent registry experience showed a learning curve with improved safety [10]. The ASAP study extended feasibility to patients considered unsuitable for warfarin, using antiplatelet-based therapy after implantation [11]. Longer-term PROTECT AF follow-up suggested reductions in haemorrhagic stroke and mortality compared with warfarin [12]. PREVAIL did not meet all prespecified efficacy non-inferiority criteria but confirmed improved procedural safety and low late stroke rates [13]. Patient-level pooled analyses supported comparable overall stroke prevention, less haemorrhagic stroke and less late major bleeding after the initial post-implant antithrombotic phase [14], [15].

Real-world data have broadened generalizability. The EWOLUTION registry reported high implant success despite older, higher-risk patients, many with contraindications to oral anticoagulation [16], and one-year outcomes showed low observed rates of ischaemic stroke and major bleeding relative to predicted risk [17]. Device-related thrombus remains clinically relevant, occurring in a minority but associated with increased embolic events; predictors include prior stroke, permanent AF, larger appendages, renal dysfunction and suboptimal antithrombotic therapy [18]. Five-year randomized data from PROTECT AF and PREVAIL reinforced durable protection, particularly against haemorrhagic stroke, while reminding clinicians that LAA closure reduces but does not abolish embolic risk [19]. PRAGUE-17, comparing LAA closure with DOACs in high-risk patients, found non-inferiority for a composite including stroke, systemic embolism, cardiovascular death, major bleeding and device/procedure complications [20].

Device technology has evolved. The Amulet IDE trial showed that the Amplatzer Amulet achieved non-inferior safety and effectiveness compared with WATCHMAN, with more complete immediate occlusion but more early procedural complications in some analyses [21]. The WATCHMAN FLX, evaluated in PINNACLE FLX, was designed for improved conformability, recapture and sealing, and showed high closure success with low serious procedure-related events [22]. Large national registries have confirmed widespread adoption and contemporary safety, while also emphasizing operator, institutional and patient-selection effects [23]. Surgical LAA occlusion during cardiac surgery reduces stroke in anticoagulated AF patients, indirectly strengthening the biologic importance of LAA exclusion, although it should not be extrapolated uncritically to percutaneous standalone therapy [24].

Several practical issues determine success. First, preprocedural imaging should define LAA ostial dimensions, depth, lobar anatomy, thrombus, septal access and neighbouring structures. Second, residual peri-device leak is common when systematically sought; small leaks are often observed, whereas larger leaks may require continued anticoagulation or reintervention, though clinically meaningful thresholds remain debated [25]. Third, post-implant antithrombotic therapy must be individualized. Original protocols used warfarin plus aspirin, followed by dual and then single antiplatelet therapy; contemporary practice increasingly uses DOACs, dual antiplatelet therapy or abbreviated regimens in selected bleeding-prone patients [26]. Fourth, non-WATCHMAN devices, including the Amplatzer Cardiac Plug/Amulet family, have substantial observational experience, particularly among patients with formal anticoagulation contraindications [27], [28].

Current consensus and guideline documents generally assign percutaneous LAA closure a role in AF patients at elevated stroke risk who have contraindications to long-term oral anticoagulation, or in carefully selected patients with recurrent major bleeding, embolic events despite adequate therapy, or strong preference after shared decision-making [29], [30]. The field is moving toward randomized comparisons against contemporary DOAC strategies, optimized antithrombotic regimens, better management of device-related thrombus and leak, and integration with AF ablation pathways. In summary, percutaneous LAA closure is no longer experimental: it is an evidence-based, device-dependent intervention that offers durable stroke prevention for selected patients, but its net benefit depends on careful imaging, procedural expertise, complication avoidance and individualized post-procedural pharmacotherapy.
